attachment.content:
- adopt-claudinite: Bootstrap Claudinite into a consuming repo — mount, hooks, checks, skills. Use when asked to bootstrap, adopt, or set up Claudinite, or to baseline a repo to pick up updates.
- adopt-pack: Add one or more packs to an already-adopted Claudinite member — declare, run each pack's adoption interview, re-vendor, scaffold, land. Use when asked to adopt, add, enable, or declare a pack (e.g. product-wiki, executable-requirements) on a repo that already runs Claudinite.
- authoring-agent-docs: How to write instruction files coding agents follow reliably. Use before writing or editing any Claude instruction doc — a project CLAUDE.md, a convention doc, a routine spec.
- bug-investigation: Method for investigating a bug and pinning down its root cause. Use when investigating a bug report, when a fix didn't hold or a bug recurs, or when a report doesn't reproduce against main.
- ci-performance-evaluation: Method for finding where a repo's CI time actually goes and what is worth fixing. Use when CI feels slow, when investigating a runtime regression, or when the weekly ci-performance task hands you a finding.
- extract-from-activity: Mine a window of a repo's commits, merged PRs and issue activity for durable, reusable lessons and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from repo artifacts — the growth-extract task's activity half, or an owner asking what a recent stretch of work taught.
- extract-from-conversations: Mine an agent-user conversation — a captured conversation log or the live session — for friction-driven lessons (misunderstandings, backtracks, measured wall-time waits) and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from a session transcript or the conversation-logs branch, or when an owner asks for a retrospective.
- file-placement: Where a file should live — the reference-distance metric, the high-reach code smell, and the mandated-location, test-location and plugin-contract exemptions. Use before placing, moving, or renaming a file, or when reviewing where one lives.
- generate-project-instructions: Decompose a project into its pack facets (working-style class, technology, aspect, domain) and extract its working instructions into reusable canon packs plus the project's own local packs (.claudinite/local_packs/). Use when a project has no established working style yet, or it exhibits a facet no pack covers — during bootstrap of a fresh/empty repo, or on an uplevel request.
- github-actions-scheduling: What a GitHub Actions `schedule:` trigger actually guarantees — late fires, dropped fires, the 60-day disable — and how to build and describe scheduled work around it. Use when adding, changing, explaining, or debugging anything that runs on a cron in GitHub Actions.
- growth-dedup: Prune a repo's local packs of items the mounted Claudinite canon now covers — remove, strip to residue, or track a wording drift, never grow an entry. Use when the growth dedup task runs, or when asked to reconcile or dedup local packs against the canon.
- prose-to-checks: Mine pack prose (RULES.md, SKILL.md) for always-testable rules that were never converted to checks, and convert the strongest ones. Use when auditing packs for convertible rules, when the weekly prose-to-checks sweep runs, or as the upgrade pass over prose a growth-extract run just wrote.
- single-issue-triage: Triage one open issue and take the first applicable action — close-if-implemented, needs-decision, blocked, quick-win, or leave. Use when acting on a single issue; "implemented in main" must be verified against main's current content and the default is to comment, not close (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-issues task hands you issues to triage).
- unattended-agents: Architecture and practices for unattended, automation-invoked agents and recurring routines. Use when building, structuring, or running an AI agent, a scheduled routine, or a multi-stage agent pipeline.
- writing-migration-plans: How to order the phases of an implementation or migration plan so nothing stalls mid-run — front-load the out-of-band setup, collapse the review gates into one stacked-PR pass, leave only executable steps — and how to keep its tracking issue append-only while implementing. Use when writing or reviewing a migration plan or a phased implementation plan, and when working through one's tracking issue.
- writing-tests: Practices for writing tests you can trust. Use before writing or changing any test — see-it-fail discipline, snapshot/golden rules, CI-only and heavy-browser tests, fuzzy-metric gating.

content.text:
Merged as [`816b138`](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/commit/816b138fcbe426ca416ce847bce6c3dbe9fcbe8e) — squash, CI green on the head sha. [#1023](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/1023) closed by the merge; local `main` synced and the squashed ref pruned; conversation captured to `conversation-logs` (506 entries) and the PR check-in cancelled.

The fix ships to members with `core` v7 on their next converge — no forcing needed, since prose delivery is uniform by construction.

Two things are still live, neither of them mine to close:

- [EdFringeNow#416](https://github.com/missingbulb/EdFringeNow/issues/416) — the Actions workflow-approval setting. Until it's flipped, that repo keeps spending each cycle landing the previous cycle's update PR, so it stays a converge behind the fleet.
- [#1025](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/1025) — `fleet-roster` still classifying by stamped-ref age. It goes from latent to noisy on **2026-08-27**, when every member crosses `staleDays: 14` against the frozen `631a067` and the sweep opens a drift issue per repo.

> ⚠️ Still open: [EdFringeNow#416](https://github.com/missingbulb/EdFringeNow/issues/416) needs your hand on the repo setting. [#1025](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/1025) is unstarted and has a hard date of 2026-08-27 — say the word and I'll take it next.

input.title: landDelivery's 180s poll gives up on a member whose slowest PR check is slower than that — and calls it "no successful run"
input.body:
`LAND_TIMEOUT_MS = 180_000` (`engine/scheduler/land-pr.mjs:426`) is premised on the comment two lines above it: *"the dispatched run this delivery just started finishes in seconds."* On a member where that is false, every update PR misses its own run's landing window and is left for the next cycle's disposal — which is the standing ~24h offset #649 existed to close, reopened for any member whose CI is slower than three minutes.

## Measured, on EdFringeNow

[Run 32090579384](https://github.com/missingbulb/EdFringeNow/actions/runs/32090579384), the run that opened [EdFringeNow#399](https://github.com/missingbulb/EdFringeNow/pull/399):

```
02:06:16  main requires nothing to merge — skipping the doomed auto-merge arm;
          waiting for this run's 2 dispatched run(s) and landing PR #399 here
02:09:19  PR #399 not landable this run (no successful run on its head sha)
          — leaving it open for the next run to dispose of
```

The two dispatched runs, both on the PR's head sha `6f8b6db`:

| workflow | started | concluded | duration |
|---|---|---|---|
| `static-site-ci.yml` | 02:06:15 | 02:06:40 | 25s, success |
| `ui-requirements.yml` | 02:06:16 | **02:09:45** | 3m29s, success |

The poll ran 02:06:16 → 02:09:19 — exactly `LAND_TIMEOUT_MS` — and gave up **26 seconds before** the second run concluded green. `pullDisposition` was correctly returning `wait` the whole time (`list.some(r => r.status !== 'completed')`), and `landAttempt` converts `wait` at timeout into `give-up`.

The next cycle's disposal then merged it, 24 hours later. Both PRs' content was green the entire time; nothing was ever wrong with the repo.

## The second defect: the message names the wrong cause

`failureSummary` (`land-pr.mjs:338-341`) has two branches — real failures, else `'no successful run on its head sha'`. A run **still in flight at the deadline** falls into the second, which reads as "CI produced nothing green" when the truth is "CI had not finished yet". That line sent me to a repository-settings diagnosis and cost a wrong issue on the member (EdFringeNow#416, closed). A timeout is not a verdict about the runs; it should say so, naming which runs were still in flight.

## Shape

- Bound the poll by what it is actually waiting for rather than by a constant premised on "seconds". The prework timeout is 900s (`packs/core/tasks/update/task.mjs`), so there is headroom to keep polling while every dispatched run is genuinely `queued`/`in_progress` and only give up when one goes red or the prework budget is nearly spent.
- Give `failureSummary` (or `landAttempt`'s caller) a distinct message for the timeout-with-runs-in-flight case, naming the workflows still running.

Note this is latent fleet-wide, not specific to one member: it fires on whichever member's slowest `pull_request` workflow crosses 180s, and nothing reports it — the member just quietly runs a cycle behind while every run reports success.

## Related

- #649 — the offset this poll was written to close.
- #677 — the "base requires nothing → skip the doomed arm, verify-then-land" path this lands in.

content.text:
**Nothing changed. There is no new flag, and [EdFringeNow#416](https://github.com/missingbulb/EdFringeNow/issues/416) was my mistake — closed as not planned.**

What went wrong in my reasoning: I quoted the `action_required` line from the 08-19 run as a fault diagnosis. It is the opposite. That string comes from `mergeReason` in [`engine/scheduler/land-pr.mjs`](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/blob/main/engine/scheduler/land-pr.mjs#L323) and is printed when a delivery **succeeds** — it explains why the merge had to bypass the arm. `action_required` is a condition the engine is explicitly designed to tolerate: it dispatches the PR's checks itself and verify-then-merges on that evidence (`land-pr.mjs:284-331`). Asking for a settings flip also ran straight into the standing decision that a platform reconfiguration is the last resort and the effect should be neutralised instead.

I had never read the run that *opened* #399. It never mentions workflow approval:

```
02:06:16  main requires nothing to merge — skipping the doomed auto-merge arm;
          waiting for this run's 2 dispatched run(s) and landing PR #399 here
02:09:19  PR #399 not landable this run (no successful run on its head sha)
          — leaving it open for the next run to dispose of
```

The real cause is a timing bound in canon. `LAND_TIMEOUT_MS` is 180s, premised on a comment saying the dispatched run "finishes in seconds". On that head sha, `static-site-ci` was green in 25s but `ui-requirements` took **3m29s** — it concluded green **26 seconds after** the poll gave up. So the poll stopped watching too early and the next cycle's disposal merged it a day later. The lag is a fixed constant meeting one member's slower CI, and it's latent for any member whose slowest `pull_request` workflow crosses 180s.

The message compounded it: `failureSummary` has no branch for "still in flight at the deadline", so it falls through to `'no successful run on its head sha'` — which reads as "CI produced nothing green" when CI simply hadn't finished. That line is what sent me to the wrong cause.

Filed as [#1026](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/1026), with both halves: bound the poll by what it's actually waiting on (there's headroom — prework's timeout is 900s), and give the timeout its own message naming the runs still in flight.

> ⚠️ Still open: [#1026](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/1026) (the real EdFringeNow cause — engine-side, unstarted) and [#1025](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/1025) (fleet-roster's ref-age measure, hard date 2026-08-27). Nothing is required of you on EdFringeNow — leave its Actions settings as they are.

Arm GitHub's native auto-merge on the PR — **squash**, always. Armed → done: GitHub lands
it once this repo's required checks pass.

## 3. When the arm is rejected

- **"Pull request is in clean status"** — the base branch requires nothing, so auto-merge
  has no queue to wait behind and this arm will be rejected every time. That is a repo
  *shape*, not an error — nothing needs fixing, and the merge is yours to make: once any
  checks that did start on the PR's head have **concluded green**, merge it yourself
  (squash). A repo with no PR checks at all merges as soon as the PR is mergeable.
- **Any other rejection** ("auto-merge is not allowed", "unstable status", …) — judge on
  evidence, exactly as the code lane's landing pass does. Read the workflow runs on the
  PR's **head sha**:
  - A run parked at `action_required` **never ran** — it is neither a pass nor a failure;
    ignore it and judge by the runs that actually executed.
  - Wait (within your run's time budget) for the real runs to conclude. Everything
    concluded, nothing failed, at least one succeeded → merge (squash).
  - Anything genuinely failed (`failure`, `timed_out`, `cancelled`, `startup_failure`),
    or the runs won't conclude inside your budget, or GitHub refuses the merge itself
    (a required gate you could not see) → **leave the PR open** and say why in your
    wrap-up comment, naming the repo settings a human should check: Settings → General →
    "Allow auto-merge", and Settings → Actions → General workflow-approval requirements
    (the usual source of the parked `action_required` run). A PR left open with its
    reason stated is a *delivered* outcome within the `merged-pr` ceiling — the trail
    survives and the task's next cycle (or the owner) picks it up; a merge past a red or
    unseen check does not survive anything.

## Never

Merge with anything but squash; merge while a real check is failing or still running;
arm or merge when the repo said `review`; write `maintenance.delivery` yourself; or
manufacture a merge to satisfy the ceiling — "no change" and "left open, reason stated"
are always legal outcomes.

input.title: Bound the landing poll by what it is waiting for, not by one number
input.head: claude/nightly-repo-updates-status-af0nq5
input.body:
Closes #1026.

`landAttempt` polled against a single `LAND_TIMEOUT_MS = 180_000` whether or not anything was observably happening, on a comment premised on "the dispatched run finishes in seconds". Two different waits were sharing one number:

- **Nothing visible yet** — a dispatch that has registered no run may never register one. Waiting long buys nothing; this keeps the 180s bound.
- **A run we can see executing** — the evidence is on its way, and the only question is whether the prework budget outlasts it. This gets its own `LAND_INFLIGHT_TIMEOUT_MS = 300_000`.

`pullDisposition`'s existing `wait` verdict is already exactly "a run is not `completed`", so the split needed no new predicate.

The in-flight bound is ceilinged by the **prework budget it spends**, not by what CI might take: the shortest `prework_timeout` among the `merged-pr` tasks is 600s, and the poll is the tail of a prework that has already converged a tree and opened a PR, so 300s leaves that preamble its room. A member whose CI outruns even this still lands next cycle — but now it says so.

## The second half: the give-up line named the wrong cause

`failureSummary` had two branches — real failures, else `'no successful run on its head sha'`. A run still in flight at the bound fell into the second, reading as "CI produced nothing green" when the truth was "CI had not finished". It now names what is still moving, and a real failure still outranks it.

## What it cost

EdFringeNow, every cycle. Its delivery dispatched two runs on the PR's head sha — `static-site-ci` green in 25s, `ui-requirements` green in **3m29s** — and the poll gave up at 183s, **26 seconds** before the second concluded. The next cycle's disposal merged it 24 hours later, so the member ran a converge behind while every run reported success. That is the standing ~24h offset #649 closed, reopened for whichever member's slowest `pull_request` workflow crosses the bound. It is latent fleet-wide, not specific to one repo.

## Verification

See-it-fail first: both new tests were written against unmodified code and failed for the right reasons — `'give-up' !== 'poll'` at 183s with a run in flight, and `failureSummary` returning `'no successful run on its head sha'`. The regression test uses the real run's timings (183s / 209s).

- `node --test engine-tests/scheduler/land-pr.test.mjs` — 46/46.
- `node --test $(git ls-files '*.test.mjs')` — 2097/2097.
- `check_the_work` clean; `check_the_world` 0 blocking, 57 advisory, none on the touched files.

One existing test changed rather than being added to: `landAttempt polls while a run is still going, and gives up at the bound` asserted give-up at `LAND_TIMEOUT_MS` for the in-flight case, which is the behaviour being fixed.

`engine/scheduler/deliver-pr.md`, the agent-lane prose twin, is unchanged on purpose: it already states the rule budget-relatively ("wait within your run's time budget", "the runs won't conclude inside your budget → leave it open and say why"), so no nuance moved there.

`ENGINE_VERSION` is untouched — it advances by release, not by an ordinary change.

The poll waits on two different things and 180s answered both. Nothing
visible is the short case — a dispatch that registered no run may never
register one. A run we can see executing is the opposite: the evidence is
coming, and the only question is whether the prework budget outlasts it.

EdFringeNow paid the difference every cycle. Its delivery dispatched two
runs, one green in 25s and one taking 3m29s; the poll gave up at 183s, 26
seconds before the second concluded green, and the next cycle's disposal
merged it a day later. That is the ~24h offset #649 closed, reopened on
whichever member's slowest pull_request workflow crosses the bound.

In-flight now has its own 300s budget, ceilinged by the prework it spends
rather than by what CI might take. And failureSummary stops reporting a
run still in flight as "no successful run on its head sha" — a timeout is
a statement about the clock, not a verdict on the runs, and conflating
them cost a wrong repository-settings diagnosis on a repo where nothing
was misconfigured.

content.text:
[#1026](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/1026) is fixed in [#1027](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/pull/1027) — [`engine/scheduler/land-pr.mjs`](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/blob/claude/nightly-repo-updates-status-af0nq5/engine/scheduler/land-pr.mjs), both halves.

**The bound.** One 180s constant was answering two different questions. Nothing-visible stays short — a dispatch that registered no run may never register one. A run we can *see* executing is the opposite case: the evidence is coming, and the only question is whether the prework budget outlasts it. That case gets its own `LAND_INFLIGHT_TIMEOUT_MS = 300_000`. `pullDisposition`'s existing `wait` verdict is already exactly "a run is not `completed`", so the split needed no new predicate. I ceilinged the new bound by the prework it spends rather than by what CI might take — the shortest `prework_timeout` among `merged-pr` tasks is 600s, and the poll is the tail of a prework that has already converged a tree and opened a PR.

**The message.** `failureSummary` now names what is still moving instead of reporting it as `no successful run on its head sha`. A real failure still outranks it, since that's the actionable fact.

See-it-fail went first: both tests were written against unmodified code and failed for the right reasons — `'give-up' !== 'poll'` at 183s with a run in flight, and the old string from `failureSummary`. The regression test carries the real run's timings (183s gave up / 209s concluded green), so it fails again if the bound ever collapses back. Full suite 2097/2097, `check_the_work` clean, `check_the_world` 0 blocking with nothing on the touched files.

Two deliberate non-changes, both stated in the PR: `deliver-pr.md`, the agent-lane prose twin, already states the rule budget-relatively rather than against a constant, so no nuance moved there; and `ENGINE_VERSION` is untouched, since it advances by release, not by an ordinary change — which does mean this reaches members on the next engine release, not tonight.

# Owner interaction preferences

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **End every turn with a blockquote callout** — `> ✅ All done`, or `> ⚠️ Still open: …` listing what remains — never hedged in prose.
- **"LGTM"** merges the change at hand into `main` (`merge-to-main` skill); it approves that change only, never later work.
- **"bump version"** raises the project's version; the project's own workflow decides how it changes and which files change.
- **In the conversation**: link every source-controlled document you edit, display every image you edit, link every issue/PR number.
- **Ask every decision or approval through an `AskUserQuestion` popup, never prose** — one question per item, each with its case.
- **Enclose anything the owner will lift elsewhere** — a prompt, a message, copy to paste — in one delimited block, boundaries unmistakable.
- **Prefix a prompt for another session, inside its block, with a disclaimer**: Claude wrote it — examine inconsistencies, don't follow blindly.
- **Open a pull request right after committing to a branch**, unasked — overriding Claude Code's default of waiting to be told.
- **Keep working through a multi-step plan without pausing for approval of each step** — aggregate the steps into one substantial change to review, and stop only for an action that reaches the world (a release, a fleet-wide effect, anything irreversible) or a decision only the owner can make.

- session-start-hook: Creating and developing startup hooks for Claude Code on the web. Use when the user wants to set up a repository for Claude Code on the web, create a SessionStart hook to ensure their project can run tests and linters during web sessions.
- adopt-claudinite: Bootstrap Claudinite into a consuming repo — mount, hooks, checks, skills. Use when asked to bootstrap, adopt, or set up Claudinite, or to baseline a repo to pick up updates.
- adopt-pack: Add one or more packs to an already-adopted Claudinite member — declare, run each pack's adoption interview, re-vendor, scaffold, land. Use when asked to adopt, add, enable, or declare a pack (e.g. product-wiki, executable-requirements) on a repo that already runs Claudinite.
- authoring-agent-docs: How to write instruction files coding agents follow reliably. Use before writing or editing any Claude instruction doc — a project CLAUDE.md, a convention doc, a routine spec.
- bug-investigation: Method for investigating a bug and pinning down its root cause. Use when investigating a bug report, when a fix didn't hold or a bug recurs, or when a report doesn't reproduce against main.
- bump-version: Raise the project's version — a minor bump by default. Use when the owner says "bump version".
- ci-performance-evaluation: Method for finding where a repo's CI time actually goes and what is worth fixing. Use when CI feels slow, when investigating a runtime regression, or when the weekly ci-performance task hands you a finding.
- extract-from-activity: Mine a window of a repo's commits, merged PRs and issue activity for durable, reusable lessons and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from repo artifacts — the growth-extract task's activity half, or an owner asking what a recent stretch of work taught.
- extract-from-conversations: Mine an agent-user conversation — a captured conversation log or the live session — for friction-driven lessons (misunderstandings, backtracks, measured wall-time waits) and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from a session transcript or the conversation-logs branch, or when an owner asks for a retrospective.
- file-placement: Where a file should live — the reference-distance metric, the high-reach code smell, and the mandated-location, test-location and plugin-contract exemptions. Use before placing, moving, or renaming a file, or when reviewing where one lives.
- generate-project-instructions: Decompose a project into its pack facets (working-style class, technology, aspect, domain) and extract its working instructions into reusable canon packs plus the project's own local packs (.claudinite/local_packs/). Use when a project has no established working style yet, or it exhibits a facet no pack covers — during bootstrap of a fresh/empty repo, or on an uplevel request.
- github-actions-scheduling: What a GitHub Actions `schedule:` trigger actually guarantees — late fires, dropped fires, the 60-day disable — and how to build and describe scheduled work around it. Use when adding, changing, explaining, or debugging anything that runs on a cron in GitHub Actions.
- growth-dedup: Prune a repo's local packs of items the mounted Claudinite canon now covers — remove, strip to residue, or track a wording drift, never grow an entry. Use when the growth dedup task runs, or when asked to reconcile or dedup local packs against the canon.
- prose-to-checks: Mine pack prose (RULES.md, SKILL.md) for always-testable rules that were never converted to checks, and convert the strongest ones. Use when auditing packs for convertible rules, when the weekly prose-to-checks sweep runs, or as the upgrade pass over prose a growth-extract run just wrote.
- repo-text-sweeps: Mechanics for grep/sed sweeps, renames, and path relocations across a repo. Use before a bulk find-replace, a rename, or moving files — and after one, to catch silently broken references.
- single-branch-status: Assess one branch's landed status — merged, already-in-main, superseded, orphaned, or genuine unmerged work — read-only. Use when triaging whether a single branch is safe to delete, judging by content not the ref's name (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-branches task hands you branches to assess).
- single-issue-triage: Triage one open issue and take the first applicable action — close-if-implemented, needs-decision, blocked, quick-win, or leave. Use when acting on a single issue; "implemented in main" must be verified against main's current content and the default is to comment, not close (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-issues task hands you issues to triage).
- single-pr-status: Assess one open pull request's landed status — keep-open, or closeable (merged, already-in-main, superseded, stale) — read-only. Use when triaging whether a single PR should stay open, judging by its commits and diff not its title (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-prs task hands you PRs to assess).
- unattended-agents: Architecture and practices for unattended, automation-invoked agents and recurring routines. Use when building, structuring, or running an AI agent, a scheduled routine, or a multi-stage agent pipeline.
- writing-claudinite-skills: Authoring or changing a skill in the Claudinite corpus — SKILL.md conventions, where a skill's checks and tests live, catalog and pack wiring. Use when creating or editing a pack's skills/<name>/ in the canon; a consumer project's own agent docs are authoring-agent-docs' turf.
- writing-migration-plans: How to order the phases of an implementation or migration plan so nothing stalls mid-run — front-load the out-of-band setup, collapse the review gates into one stacked-PR pass, leave only executable steps — and how to keep its tracking issue append-only while implementing. Use when writing or reviewing a migration plan or a phased implementation plan, and when working through one's tracking issue.
- writing-tests: Practices for writing tests you can trust. Use before writing or changing any test — see-it-fail discipline, snapshot/golden rules, CI-only and heavy-browser tests, fuzzy-metric gating.
- design: Create a design canvas — a multi-artboard visual design published as an Artifact that runs Claude Design's canvas editor (an early preview of Claude Design inside Claude Code). You DRAFT the design as .dc.html artboards laid out on one pan/zoom canvas; where saving is enabled for the user's account they refine every element visually (click-to-select, a properties panel, inline text editing, undo/redo) and Save publishes a new version for everyone, otherwise they get a view-and-export (PNG/PDF) preview of your draft. Good for UI mockups and screen flows, landing pages, marketing and social graphics, and print pieces — posters, flyers, brochures as single-page artboards; memos and reports as one flowing artboard. Use when someone wants a design, mockup, wireframe, UI or screen design, landing page, poster, flyer, brochure, banner, card, one-pager, or any visual layout they would rather tweak by hand than in code. Only for CREATING or re-seeding a canvas; an existing one is edited in its published Artifact.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including Markdown ones — format is part of the design pass, never a speed shortcut.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts — when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, keeping state shared across viewers, handing the viewer a file to save, or updating and republishing itself. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. {"number":1027,"title":"Bound the landing poll by what it is waiting for, not by one number","body":"Closes #1026.

`landAttempt` polled against a single `LAND_TIMEOUT_MS = 180_000` whether or not anything was observably happening, on a comment premised on "the dispatched run finishes in seconds". Two different waits were sharing one number:

- **Nothing visible yet** — a dispatch that has registered no run may never register one. Waiting long buys nothing; this keeps the 180s bound.
- **A run we can see executing** — the evidence is on its way, and the only question is whether the prework budget outlasts it. This gets its own `LAND_INFLIGHT_TIMEOUT_MS = 300_000`.

`pullDisposition`'s existing `wait` verdict is already exactly "a run is not `completed`", so the split needed no new predicate.

The in-flight bound is ceilinged by the **prework budget it spends**, not by what CI might take: the shortest `prework_timeout` among the `merged-pr` tasks is 600s, and the poll is the tail of a prework that has already converged a tree and opened a PR, so 300s leaves that preamble its room. A member whose CI outruns even this still lands next cycle — but now it says so.

## The second half: the give-up line named the wrong cause

`failureSummary` had two branches — real failures, else `'no successful run on its head sha'`. A run still in flight at the bound fell into the second, reading as "CI produced nothing green" when the truth was "CI had not finished". It now names what is still moving, and a real failure still outranks it.

## What it cost

EdFringeNow, every cycle. Its delivery dispatched two runs on the PR's head sha — `static-site-ci` green in 25s, `ui-requirements` green in **3m29s** — and the poll gave up at 183s, **26 seconds** before the second concluded. The next cycle's disposal merged it 24 hours later, so the member ran a converge behind while every run reported success. That is the standing ~24h offset #649 closed, reopened for whichever member's slowest `pull_request` workflow crosses the bound. It is latent fleet-wide, not specific to one repo.

## Verification

See-it-fail first: both new tests were written against unmodified code and failed for the right reasons — `'give-up' !== 'poll'` at 183s with a run in flight, and `failureSummary` returning `'no successful run on its head sha'`. The regression test uses the real run's timings (183s / 209s).

- `node --test engine-tests/scheduler/land-pr.test.mjs` — 46/46.
- `node --test $(git ls-files '*.test.mjs')` — 2097/2097.
- `check_the_work` clean; `check_the_world` 0 blocking, 57 advisory, none on the touched files.

One existing test changed rather than being added to: `landAttempt polls while a run is still going, and gives up at the bound` asserted give-up at `LAND_TIMEOUT_MS` for the in-flight case, which is the behaviour being fixed.

`engine/scheduler/deliver-pr.md`, the agent-lane prose twin, is unchanged on purpose: it already states the rule budget-relatively ("wait within your run's time budget", "the runs won't conclude inside your budget → leave it open and say why"), so no nuance moved there.

`ENGINE_VERSION` is untouched — it advances by release, not by an ordinary change.

the landing poll by what it is waiting for, not by one number

The poll waits on two different things and 180s answered both. Nothing
visible is the short case — a dispatch that registered no run may never
register one. A run we can see executing is the opposite: the evidence is
coming, and the only question is whether the prework budget outlasts it.

EdFringeNow paid the difference every cycle. Its delivery dispatched two
runs, one green in 25s and one taking 3m29s; the poll gave up at 183s, 26
seconds before the second concluded green, and the next cycle's disposal
merged it a day later. That is the ~24h offset #649 closed, reopened on
whichever member's slowest pull_request workflow crosses the bound.

In-flight now has its own 300s budget, ceilinged by the prework it spends
rather than by what CI might take. And failureSummary stops reporting a
run still in flight as "no successful run on its head sha" — a timeout is
a statement about the clock, not a verdict on the runs, and conflating
them cost a wrong repository-settings diagnosis on a repo where nothing
was misconfigured.

# Owner interaction preferences

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **End every turn with a blockquote callout** — `> ✅ All done`, or `> ⚠️ Still open: …` listing what remains — never hedged in prose.
- **"LGTM"** merges the change at hand into `main` (`merge-to-main` skill); it approves that change only, never later work.
- **"bump version"** raises the project's version; the project's own workflow decides how it changes and which files change.
- **In the conversation**: link every source-controlled document you edit, display every image you edit, link every issue/PR number.
- **Ask every decision or approval through an `AskUserQuestion` popup, never prose** — one question per item, each with its case.
- **Enclose anything the owner will lift elsewhere** — a prompt, a message, copy to paste — in one delimited block, boundaries unmistakable.
- **Prefix a prompt for another session, inside its block, with a disclaimer**: Claude wrote it — examine inconsistencies, don't follow blindly.

# Owner interaction preferences

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. ## Preferences

- **"LGTM"** merges the change at hand into `main` (`merge-to-main` skill); it approves that change only, never later work.

{"number":1027,"title":"Bound the landing poll by what it is waiting for, not by one number","body":"Closes #1026.

`landAttempt` polled against a single `LAND_TIMEOUT_MS = 180_000` whether or not anything was observably happening, on a comment premised on "the dispatched run finishes in seconds". Two different waits were sharing one number:

- **Nothing visible yet** — a dispatch that has registered no run may never register one. Waiting long buys nothing; this keeps the 180s bound.
- **A run we can see executing** — the evidence is on its way, and the only question is whether the prework budget outlasts it. This gets its own `LAND_INFLIGHT_TIMEOUT_MS = 300_000`.

`pullDisposition`'s existing `wait` verdict is already exactly "a run is not `completed`", so the split needed no new predicate.

The in-flight bound is ceilinged by the **prework budget it spends**, not by what CI might take: the shortest `prework_timeout` among the `merged-pr` tasks is 600s, and the poll is the tail of a prework that has already converged a tree and opened a PR, so 300s leaves that preamble its room. A member whose CI outruns even this still lands next cycle — but now it says so.

## The second half: the give-up line named the wrong cause

`failureSummary` had two branches — real failures, else `'no successful run on its head sha'`. A run still in flight at the bound fell into the second, reading as "CI produced nothing green" when the truth was "CI had not finished". It now names what is still moving, and a real failure still outranks it.

## What it cost

EdFringeNow, every cycle. Its delivery dispatched two runs on the PR's head sha — `static-site-ci` green in 25s, `ui-requirements` green in **3m29s** — and the poll gave up at 183s, **26 seconds** before the second concluded. The next cycle's disposal merged it 24 hours later, so the member ran a converge behind while every run reported success. That is the standing ~24h offset #649 closed, reopened for whichever member's slowest `pull_request` workflow crosses the bound. It is latent fleet-wide, not specific to one repo.

## Verification

See-it-fail first: both new tests were written against unmodified code and failed for the right reasons — `'give-up' !== 'poll'` at 183s with a run in flight, and `failureSummary` returning `'no successful run on its head sha'`. The regression test uses the real run's timings (183s / 209s).

- `node --test engine-tests/scheduler/land-pr.test.mjs` — 46/46.
- `node --test $(git ls-files '*.test.mjs')` — 2097/2097.
- `check_the_work` clean; `check_the_world` 0 blocking, 57 advisory, none on the touched files.

One existing test changed rather than being added to: `landAttempt polls while a run is still going, and gives up at the bound` asserted give-up at `LAND_TIMEOUT_MS` for the in-flight case, which is the behaviour being fixed.

`engine/scheduler/deliver-pr.md`, the agent-lane prose twin, is unchanged on purpose: it already states the rule budget-relatively ("wait within your run's time budget", "the runs won't conclude inside your budget → leave it open and say why"), so no nuance moved there.

`ENGINE_VERSION` is untouched — it advances by release, not by an ordinary change.

{"number":1027,"title":"Bound the landing poll by what it is waiting for, not by one number","body":"Closes #1026.

`landAttempt` polled against a single `LAND_TIMEOUT_MS = 180_000` whether or not anything was observably happening, on a comment premised on "the dispatched run finishes in seconds". Two different waits were sharing one number:

- **Nothing visible yet** — a dispatch that has registered no run may never register one. Waiting long buys nothing; this keeps the 180s bound.
- **A run we can see executing** — the evidence is on its way, and the only question is whether the prework budget outlasts it. This gets its own `LAND_INFLIGHT_TIMEOUT_MS = 300_000`.

`pullDisposition`'s existing `wait` verdict is already exactly "a run is not `completed`", so the split needed no new predicate.

The in-flight bound is ceilinged by the **prework budget it spends**, not by what CI might take: the shortest `prework_timeout` among the `merged-pr` tasks is 600s, and the poll is the tail of a prework that has already converged a tree and opened a PR, so 300s leaves that preamble its room. A member whose CI outruns even this still lands next cycle — but now it says so.

## The second half: the give-up line named the wrong cause

`failureSummary` had two branches — real failures, else `'no successful run on its head sha'`. A run still in flight at the bound fell into the second, reading as "CI produced nothing green" when the truth was "CI had not finished". It now names what is still moving, and a real failure still outranks it.

## What it cost

EdFringeNow, every cycle. Its delivery dispatched two runs on the PR's head sha — `static-site-ci` green in 25s, `ui-requirements` green in **3m29s** — and the poll gave up at 183s, **26 seconds** before the second concluded. The next cycle's disposal merged it 24 hours later, so the member ran a converge behind while every run reported success. That is the standing ~24h offset #649 closed, reopened for whichever member's slowest `pull_request` workflow crosses the bound. It is latent fleet-wide, not specific to one repo.

## Verification

See-it-fail first: both new tests were written against unmodified code and failed for the right reasons — `'give-up' !== 'poll'` at 183s with a run in flight, and `failureSummary` returning `'no successful run on its head sha'`. The regression test uses the real run's timings (183s / 209s).

- `node --test engine-tests/scheduler/land-pr.test.mjs` — 46/46.
- `node --test $(git ls-files '*.test.mjs')` — 2097/2097.
- `check_the_work` clean; `check_the_world` 0 blocking, 57 advisory, none on the touched files.

One existing test changed rather than being added to: `landAttempt polls while a run is still going, and gives up at the bound` asserted give-up at `LAND_TIMEOUT_MS` for the in-flight case, which is the behaviour being fixed.

`engine/scheduler/deliver-pr.md`, the agent-lane prose twin, is unchanged on purpose: it already states the rule budget-relatively ("wait within your run's time budget", "the runs won't conclude inside your budget → leave it open and say why"), so no nuance moved there.

`ENGINE_VERSION` is untouched — it advances by release, not by an ordinary change.

{"number":1027,"title":"Bound the landing poll by what it is waiting for, not by one number","body":"Closes #1026.

`landAttempt` polled against a single `LAND_TIMEOUT_MS = 180_000` whether or not anything was observably happening, on a comment premised on "the dispatched run finishes in seconds". Two different waits were sharing one number:

- **Nothing visible yet** — a dispatch that has registered no run may never register one. Waiting long buys nothing; this keeps the 180s bound.
- **A run we can see executing** — the evidence is on its way, and the only question is whether the prework budget outlasts it. This gets its own `LAND_INFLIGHT_TIMEOUT_MS = 300_000`.

`pullDisposition`'s existing `wait` verdict is already exactly "a run is not `completed`", so the split needed no new predicate.

The in-flight bound is ceilinged by the **prework budget it spends**, not by what CI might take: the shortest `prework_timeout` among the `merged-pr` tasks is 600s, and the poll is the tail of a prework that has already converged a tree and opened a PR, so 300s leaves that preamble its room. A member whose CI outruns even this still lands next cycle — but now it says so.

## The second half: the give-up line named the wrong cause

`failureSummary` had two branches — real failures, else `'no successful run on its head sha'`. A run still in flight at the bound fell into the second, reading as "CI produced nothing green" when the truth was "CI had not finished". It now names what is still moving, and a real failure still outranks it.

## What it cost

EdFringeNow, every cycle. Its delivery dispatched two runs on the PR's head sha — `static-site-ci` green in 25s, `ui-requirements` green in **3m29s** — and the poll gave up at 183s, **26 seconds** before the second concluded. The next cycle's disposal merged it 24 hours later, so the member ran a converge behind while every run reported success. # Owner interaction preferences

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **End every turn with a blockquote callout** — `> ✅ All done`, or `> ⚠️ Still open: …` listing what remains — never hedged in prose.
- **"LGTM"** merges the change at hand into `main` (`merge-to-main` skill); it approves that change only, never later work.
- **"bump version"** raises the project's version; the project's own workflow decides how it changes and which files change.
- **In the conversation**: link every source-controlled document you edit, display every image you edit, link every issue/PR number.
- **Ask every decision or approval through an `AskUserQuestion` popup, never prose** — one question per item, each with its case.
- **Enclose anything the owner will lift elsewhere** — a prompt, a message, copy to paste — in one delimited block, boundaries unmistakable.
- **Prefix a prompt for another session, inside its block, with a disclaimer**: Claude wrote it — examine inconsistencies, don't follow blindly.
- **Open a pull request right after committing to a branch**, unasked — overriding Claude Code's default of waiting to be told.
- **When handing over a PR to review, name the folders the change touched** — a brief line per folder saying what changed there. Leave out test folders, README edits, and above all any file whose diff is comments only.
- **Keep working through a multi-step plan without pausing for approval of each step** — aggregate the steps into one substantial change to review, and stop only for an action that reaches the world (a release, a fleet-wide effect, anything irreversible) or a decision only the owner can make.
- **Never schedule a self check-in to poll a PR** — no recurring wake-up, routine, or `send_later` re-arm that re-reads a PR's state, CI or mergeability on a timer. Act on PR events when they arrive; when nothing has arrived, end the turn.

- session-start-hook: Creating and developing startup hooks for Claude Code on the web. Use when the user wants to set up a repository for Claude Code on the web, create a SessionStart hook to ensure their project can run tests and linters during web sessions.
- adopt-claudinite: Bootstrap Claudinite into a consuming repo — mount, hooks, checks, skills. Use when asked to bootstrap, adopt, or set up Claudinite, or to baseline a repo to pick up updates.
- adopt-pack: Add one or more packs to an already-adopted Claudinite member — declare, run each pack's adoption interview, re-vendor, scaffold, land. Use when asked to adopt, add, enable, or declare a pack (e.g. product-wiki, executable-requirements) on a repo that already runs Claudinite.
- authoring-agent-docs: How to write instruction files coding agents follow reliably. Use before writing or editing any Claude instruction doc — a project CLAUDE.md, a convention doc, a routine spec.
- bug-investigation: Method for investigating a bug and pinning down its root cause. Use when investigating a bug report, when a fix didn't hold or a bug recurs, or when a report doesn't reproduce against main.
- bump-version: Raise the project's version — a minor bump by default. Use when the owner says "bump version".
- ci-performance-evaluation: Method for finding where a repo's CI time actually goes and what is worth fixing. Use when CI feels slow, when investigating a runtime regression, or when the weekly ci-performance task hands you a finding.
- extract-from-activity: Mine a window of a repo's commits, merged PRs and issue activity for durable, reusable lessons and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from repo artifacts — the growth-extract task's activity half, or an owner asking what a recent stretch of work taught.
- extract-from-conversations: Mine an agent-user conversation — a captured conversation log or the live session — for friction-driven lessons (misunderstandings, backtracks, measured wall-time waits) and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from a session transcript or the conversation-logs branch, or when an owner asks for a retrospective.
- file-placement: Where a file should live — the reference-distance metric, the high-reach code smell, and the mandated-location, test-location and plugin-contract exemptions. Use before placing, moving, or renaming a file, or when reviewing where one lives.
- generate-project-instructions: Decompose a project into its pack facets (working-style class, technology, aspect, domain) and extract its working instructions into reusable canon packs plus the project's own local packs (.claudinite/local_packs/). Use when a project has no established working style yet, or it exhibits a facet no pack covers — during bootstrap of a fresh/empty repo, or on an uplevel request.
- github-actions-scheduling: What a GitHub Actions `schedule:` trigger actually guarantees — late fires, dropped fires, the 60-day disable — and how to build and describe scheduled work around it. Use when adding, changing, explaining, or debugging anything that runs on a cron in GitHub Actions.
- growth-dedup: Prune a repo's local packs of items the mounted Claudinite canon now covers — remove, strip to residue, or track a wording drift, never grow an entry. Use when the growth dedup task runs, or when asked to reconcile or dedup local packs against the canon.
- prose-to-checks: Mine pack prose (RULES.md, SKILL.md) for always-testable rules that were never converted to checks, and convert the strongest ones. Use when auditing packs for convertible rules, when the weekly prose-to-checks sweep runs, or as the upgrade pass over prose a growth-extract run just wrote.
- repo-text-sweeps: Mechanics for grep/sed sweeps, renames, and path relocations across a repo. Use before a bulk find-replace, a rename, or moving files — and after one, to catch silently broken references.
- single-branch-status: Assess one branch's landed status — merged, already-in-main, superseded, orphaned, or genuine unmerged work — read-only. Use when triaging whether a single branch is safe to delete, judging by content not the ref's name (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-branches task hands you branches to assess).
- single-issue-triage: Triage one open issue and take the first applicable action — close-if-implemented, needs-decision, blocked, quick-win, or leave. Use when acting on a single issue; "implemented in main" must be verified against main's current content and the default is to comment, not close (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-issues task hands you issues to triage).
- single-pr-status: Assess one open pull request's landed status — keep-open, or closeable (merged, already-in-main, superseded, stale) — read-only. Use when triaging whether a single PR should stay open, judging by its commits and diff not its title (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-prs task hands you PRs to assess).
- unattended-agents: Architecture and practices for unattended, automation-invoked agents and recurring routines. Use when building, structuring, or running an AI agent, a scheduled routine, or a multi-stage agent pipeline.
- writing-claudinite-skills: Authoring or changing a skill in the Claudinite corpus — SKILL.md conventions, where a skill's checks and tests live, catalog and pack wiring. Use when creating or editing a pack's skills/<name>/ in the canon; a consumer project's own agent docs are authoring-agent-docs' turf.
- writing-migration-plans: How to order the phases of an implementation or migration plan so nothing stalls mid-run — front-load the out-of-band setup, collapse the review gates into one stacked-PR pass, leave only executable steps — and how to keep its tracking issue append-only while implementing. Use when writing or reviewing a migration plan or a phased implementation plan, and when working through one's tracking issue.
- writing-tests: Practices for writing tests you can trust. Use before writing or changing any test — see-it-fail discipline, snapshot/golden rules, CI-only and heavy-browser tests, fuzzy-metric gating.
- design: Create a design canvas — a multi-artboard visual design published as an Artifact that runs Claude Design's canvas editor (an early preview of Claude Design inside Claude Code). You DRAFT the design as .dc.html artboards laid out on one pan/zoom canvas; where saving is enabled for the user's account they refine every element visually (click-to-select, a properties panel, inline text editing, undo/redo) and Save publishes a new version for everyone, otherwise they get a view-and-export (PNG/PDF) preview of your draft. Good for UI mockups and screen flows, landing pages, marketing and social graphics, and print pieces — posters, flyers, brochures as single-page artboards; memos and reports as one flowing artboard. Use when someone wants a design, mockup, wireframe, UI or screen design, landing page, poster, flyer, brochure, banner, card, one-pager, or any visual layout they would rather tweak by hand than in code. Only for CREATING or re-seeding a canvas; an existing one is edited in its published Artifact.

Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. - artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, keeping state shared across viewers, handing the viewer a file to save, or updating and republishing itself. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
